description: Directive (EU) 2017/1132 relating to certain aspects of company law, codifying previous company law directives into a single instrument. Covers formation, capital, mergers, divisions, and cross-border mergers of limited liability companies. The foundational EU company law text.

Directive (EU) 2019/2121 amending Directive 2017/1132 as regards cross-border conversions, mergers and divisions. Introduces harmonised procedures for cross-border conversions and divisions for the first time. Includes anti-abuse safeguards and employee protection measures.

Directive (EU) 2017/828 amending Directive 2007/36/EC as regards the encouragement of long-term shareholder engagement. Strengthens shareholder identification, say-on-pay votes, related-party transaction oversight, and proxy advisor transparency. Key governance instrument for listed companies.

Directive 2007/36/EC on the exercise of certain rights of shareholders in listed companies. Establishes minimum rights for shareholders regarding general meetings, proxy voting, and information access. Foundation upon which SRD II builds.

Directive 2009/102/EC on single-member private limited-liability companies, codifying Twelfth Company Law Directive. Requires Member States to allow formation of single-member companies and sets disclosure requirements for sole shareholder status.

Directive (EU) 2019/1151 amending Directive 2017/1132 as regards the use of digital tools and processes in company law. Requires Member States to allow online company formation, online filing of documents, and interconnection of business registers (BRIS). Reduces administrative burden.

Directive 2004/25/EC on takeover bids, establishing minimum rules for mandatory and voluntary public takeover offers. Covers mandatory bid threshold, squeeze-out and sell-out rights, board neutrality rule, and breakthrough rule. Member States may opt out of key provisions.

Council Regulation (EC) No 2157/2001 on the Statute for a European company (SE). Allows companies incorporated in different Member States to merge or form a holding company or joint subsidiary under a single European legal form. Requires employee involvement arrangements.

Council Regulation (EC) No 1435/2003 on the Statute for a European Cooperative Society (SCE). Enables cooperatives from different Member States to form a European-level cooperative. Governed by similar principles as the SE Statute with cooperative-specific modifications.

Directive 2013/34/EU on the annual financial statements, consolidated financial statements and related reports. Sets rules for company size categories, accounting formats, and disclosure obligations. Underpins corporate transparency and capital maintenance rules.

The fundamental obligation of directors to act in good faith, in the best interests of the company, and with due care, skill, and diligence. While primarily governed by national law, EU instruments reference and reinforce these duties, particularly in the context of related-party transactions and shareholder engagement.

The obligation of directors to exercise reasonable care, skill, and diligence in managing the company. Assessed against the standard of a reasonably diligent person with the same knowledge, skill, and experience. Breach may give rise to personal liability.

The obligation of directors to act in the best interests of the company, avoiding conflicts of interest and not appropriating corporate opportunities. Requires disclosure of personal interests in transactions. Breach may result in disgorgement of profits and personal liability.

A legal principle providing directors with a safe harbour for business decisions made in good faith, on an informed basis, and in the honest belief that the decision serves the company's best interests. Widely recognised across EU Member States in varying forms. Prevents courts from second-guessing reasonable business decisions.

metadata.origin: common law, widely adopted in civil law jurisdictions

description: The legal exposure of directors to personal liability for breach of duties, including liability to the company (internal liability), to creditors in insolvency situations, and to third parties in cases of fraud or gross negligence. Governed primarily by national company law but influenced by EU frameworks.

The supreme decision-making body of a company where shareholders exercise their voting rights. EU law (SRD I and II) sets minimum standards for convening, information provision, proxy voting, and electronic participation. Annual general meetings must approve annual accounts and elect/discharge directors.

The right of shareholders to vote at general meetings, typically proportional to shareholding. EU law establishes the one-share-one-vote principle as a default for listed companies. Includes rights to vote by proxy, electronically, and across borders. Dual-class share structures remain permitted in some jurisdictions.

Legal safeguards for minority shareholders against expropriation by controlling shareholders or management. Includes rights to call special meetings, appraisal rights, derivative actions, anti-dilution protections, and squeeze-out/sell-out mechanisms. Addressed across multiple EU directives.

Requirement under SRD II for listed companies to submit the remuneration policy to a binding shareholder vote at least every four years, and the annual remuneration report to an advisory vote. Ensures shareholder oversight of executive compensation. Non-compliance requires explanation.

SRD II requires listed companies to publicly announce material related-party transactions at the time of conclusion and to submit them for approval by the board or shareholders. Aims to prevent value extraction by controlling shareholders or insiders. Thresholds and approval mechanisms determined by Member States.

Situations where a director's personal interests may conflict with their duty to act in the company's best interests. EU corporate governance frameworks require disclosure, recusal from voting, and in some cases prior authorisation. Related-party transaction rules in SRD II provide a specific regime for listed companies.

The EU framework of comply-or-explain corporate governance codes applied in each Member State. While no single EU governance code exists, the EU requires listed companies to refer to a national code and disclose compliance or explain deviations. Key areas: board composition, audit committees, remuneration, risk management.

EU framework on board composition covering one-tier and two-tier board structures recognised across Member States. Includes requirements for independent directors, diversity targets (Directive 2022/2381 on gender balance), and separation of chair/CEO roles. Corporate governance codes further specify best practices.

canonical_name: Gender Balance on Company Boards Directive (EU) 2022/2381
description: Directive (EU) 2022/2381 on improving the gender balance among directors of listed companies. Requires listed companies to achieve at least 40% of non-executive director positions or 33% of all director positions held by the under-represented sex by 30 June 2026. Applies to listed companies in all Member States.

The EU legal framework requiring companies to maintain minimum capital levels to protect creditors. Codified in Directive 2017/1132 (originally Second Company Law Directive). Includes rules on minimum share capital, restrictions on distributions, prohibition of financial assistance, and mandatory capital reduction procedures.

EU company law prohibits distributions to shareholders that would reduce net assets below subscribed capital plus undistributable reserves. Dividends may only be paid from distributable profits. Interim dividends permitted subject to conditions. Member States may impose additional restrictions.

metadata.test: net assets >= subscribed capital + undistributable reserves

canonical_name: Share Buyback and Treasury Share Rules
description: Directive 2017/1132 permits public limited companies to acquire their own shares subject to conditions: shareholder authorisation, maximum 10% of subscribed capital, acquisition from distributable profits only, and mandatory treasury share restrictions including suspension of voting rights. Prevents capital erosion and market manipulation.

Directive 2017/1132 prohibits public limited companies from providing financial assistance (loans, guarantees, security) for the acquisition of their own shares. Prevents leveraged acquisitions at the company's expense. Some Member States provide whitewash procedures with safeguards.

metadata.exceptions: whitewash procedures in some Member States

canonical_name: Serious Loss of Capital — Mandatory Meeting
description: Directive 2017/1132 requires that where the net assets of a public limited company fall below half the subscribed capital, the directors must convene a general meeting to decide on the company's future (continuation, capital reduction, or winding up). A critical creditor protection mechanism.

The harmonised procedure under Directive 2017/1132 (as amended by 2019/2121) for merging limited liability companies across EU Member States. Involves common draft terms, independent expert report, shareholder approval, creditor and employee protection, and legality certificate from national authority. Simplified procedure available for wholly-owned subsidiaries.

Introduced by Directive 2019/2121, this allows a company to convert into a legal form governed by the law of another Member State while retaining legal personality. Includes anti-abuse checks, independent expert assessment, shareholder cash compensation rights, and employee participation protections.

metadata.anti_abuse: competent authority may refuse if arrangement is artificial

description: Introduced by Directive 2019/2121, this harmonises procedures for cross-border divisions (full division, partial division, and division by separation). Includes common draft terms, independent expert report, shareholder approval, creditor protection, and employee participation safeguards.

metadata.legal_basis: Directive 2017/1132 Title II Chapter IV (inserted by 2019/2121)

description: Directive 2019/2121 introduces a substantive anti-abuse check by the competent authority of the departure Member State. The authority may refuse a pre-operation certificate if the cross-border operation constitutes an artificial arrangement aimed at obtaining undue tax advantages or unduly prejudicing creditors, employees, or minority shareholders.

canonical_name: Corporate Group Structures in EU Law
description: EU company law recognises parent-subsidiary relationships but lacks a comprehensive group law directive. Groups are regulated through consolidated accounting (Directive 2013/34/EU), cross-border merger rules, and the acquis on related-party transactions. Some Member States (notably Germany with Konzernrecht) have comprehensive national group law.

Parent undertakings must prepare consolidated financial statements and a consolidated management report under Directive 2013/34/EU. Consolidation is required when the parent has a majority of voting rights, the right to appoint/remove a majority of the board, or exercises dominant influence. Exemptions exist for small groups.

The right of a majority shareholder holding 90% or more of the voting rights (or such higher threshold as set by Member States, up to 95%) to compulsorily acquire the remaining shares. Governed by the Takeover Directive (2004/25/EC) in takeover contexts and by national company law generally. Minority shareholders receive fair price.

The reciprocal right of minority shareholders to require the majority shareholder to purchase their shares at a fair price when the majority holder has acquired 90% or more of voting rights. Protects minorities locked into a company with a dominant shareholder. Provided by the Takeover Directive.

Under the Takeover Directive, any natural or legal person who acquires control of a listed company (as defined by national law, typically 30-33% of voting rights) must make a mandatory offer to all remaining shareholders at an equitable price. Protects minority shareholders from control changes without exit opportunity.

metadata.price: equitable price (highest price paid in preceding period)

description: The Takeover Directive requires that once a takeover bid is announced, the board of the target company must obtain prior shareholder authorisation before taking any action that could frustrate the bid (defensive measures). Member States may opt out of this rule. Aims to protect shareholder decision-making.

An optional provision of the Takeover Directive allowing a bidder who has acquired 75% of capital to break through certain pre-bid defences (restrictions on transfer, voting caps, special rights) at the first general meeting post-bid. Few Member States have adopted this rule.

The EU-wide interconnection of business registers established under Directive 2017/1132. Enables cross-border access to company information, disclosure of branch and subsidiary data, and electronic communication between registers. Enhanced by the Digitalisation Directive 2019/1151.

Directive 2019/1151 requires Member States to enable fully online formation of certain company types (at minimum, private limited liability companies), including identity verification, articles of association templates, and online filing. Reduces formation time and cost for entrepreneurs.

metadata.maximum_time: 5 working days (or 10 if manual verification needed)

description: SRD II grants listed companies the right to identify their shareholders through the intermediary chain (custodians, CSDs). Intermediaries must transmit shareholder information upon request. Enables issuers to communicate directly with shareholders and facilitates exercise of shareholder rights across borders.

SRD II requires proxy advisors to publicly disclose their code of conduct, methodology, and sources of information used for voting recommendations. Aims to address conflicts of interest and ensure quality of proxy advice. Applies a comply-or-explain approach.

SRD II requires institutional investors and asset managers to develop and publicly disclose an engagement policy describing how they integrate shareholder engagement into their investment strategy, monitor investee companies, and exercise voting rights. Comply-or-explain basis.

SRD II requires listed companies to establish a clear remuneration policy for directors, subject to a binding shareholder vote at least every four years. The policy must explain how it contributes to business strategy, long-term interests, and sustainability, and set maximum remuneration levels.

SRD II requires listed companies to draw up a clear and understandable annual remuneration report providing a comprehensive overview of individual director remuneration. Subject to an advisory shareholder vote at the annual general meeting. Must explain how the remuneration policy was applied.

EU company law protects employee participation rights (board-level representation and information/consultation) in cross-border mergers, conversions, and divisions. Directive 2019/2121 ensures that cross-border mobility cannot be used to circumvent existing employee participation arrangements. Negotiation procedure applies.

The European Commission's Directorate-General for Justice and Consumers is responsible for EU company law policy, including proposing new legislation, monitoring transposition, and enforcement through infringement proceedings. The Commission also manages the BRIS interconnection system.

An expert advisory group established by the European Commission to provide advice on EU company law matters. Composed of independent academics and practitioners. Has produced reports on digitalisation, cross-border mobility, and group law that have influenced legislative proposals.

Directive 2017/1132 harmonises minimum formation requirements for public limited companies including memorandum and articles of association, minimum capital subscription, independent valuation of non-cash contributions, and registration in the business register. The Digitalisation Directive extends this to online formation.

EU company law requires qualified majority shareholder approval (typically two-thirds of capital represented, but Member States may require higher) for fundamental corporate decisions: amendments to articles, capital changes, mergers, divisions, and winding up. Protects minority shareholders from simple majority decisions on existential matters.

The Takeover Directive requires Member States to set a threshold at which acquisition of voting rights in a listed company triggers a mandatory bid obligation. Most Member States set this at 30% or 33% of voting rights. Some allow creeping-in provisions. The exact threshold is determined by national law.

The Takeover Directive allows Member States to set the squeeze-out threshold between 90% and 95% of voting rights and capital. At this level, the majority holder may compulsorily acquire remaining shares. Member States have chosen different levels within this range.
